Using data collected by the LHCb experiment at the LHC, the effective $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ lifespan has been assessed, taking into account the time-dependent $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay rate, which depends on $m_B^0$ and can be attributed to $B^0_s$-$\bar B^0_s$ mixing. By applying a likelihood fit to naturally logarithmically linearized $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay rates, the decay rate width has been derived as $x_{BS}=\bigg(\frac{\Gamma(B^0_s\rightarrow f)}{\Gamma(B^0_s\rightarrow \bar B^0_s\rightarrow f)}\bigg)^{1/2}=\frac{\Gamma_{B^0_s}}{m_{B^0_s}}$. Utilizing the LHCb collaboration's previous $\ K^+K^-$ candidate datasets, which encompass both $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ neutral and charged charge-conjugate decays, a result has been obtained, leading to $\Gamma_{B^0_s}/m_{B^0_s} = 0.469 \pm 0.026 (\mathrm{stat.}) \pm 0.011 (\mathrm{sys.}) \, \mathrm{ps}^{-1

We performed numerical experiments to investigate the numerical method proposed by our team for solving a problem it struggles to address effectively in real-time, due to its ability to accurately represent a complex, unpredictable phenomenon it experiences daily. Our method successfully represented the problem's spread and a related, constantly changing geographic feature whose shape and location are in a state of flux. By combining it with a state-of-the-art solver for representing the unpredictable feature's behavior, it was able to accurately simulate its effects on the problem's distribution across the region.

At high energies, the source of the extreme variability in the direction of cosmic rays remains highly speculative. The Pierre Auger Observatory's vast 2,700 square kilometer detection area and its ten-year operation provide a comprehensive view of the sky for cosmic rays with energies exceeding 4 EeV. A detailed study of large-scale patterns in the distribution of these ultra-high-energy cosmic rays in the Southern Hemisphere has been conducted using 4000 events. The analysis reveals striking anisotropies, with the source of UHECRs potentially confined to a specific region of the galaxy or even a smaller, unknown galaxy in the Local Group. The research also suggests the presence of large-scale dipole and quadrupole effects and identifies smaller anisotropies in specific energy ranges and in smaller energy bands in different parts of the sky. The results obtained in this analysis may be influenced by systematic errors associated with the detection method, model calculations of shower development, local magnetic field effects, and the Earth's influence on charged super-gamma rays, with possible implications for further studies of the nature of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays.
This paper provides a proof that Zinbiel algebras possess a specific property known as solvability.

A study was conducted to analyze the average flow vector components, namely magnitude ($v_n$) and phase ($\phi_n$), for various harmonics (n = 2, 3) in lead-lead collisions at the LHC. These collisions took place with a midrapidity multiplicity ($\langle N_{\rm ch}\rangle$) of approximately 6000. To isolate the influence of symmetry, only central collisions from even-numbered events were considered. Findings revealed that the second harmonic's phase relates positively to the beam direction and is unaffected by collisions' centrality, whereas central collisions with odd-numbered events introduce a negative second harmonic's phase. Additionally, a theoretical model called AMPT accurately replicated observed data.

This research focuses on resolving differences in tables that have null values and functional dependencies, which are crucial elements often overlooked when exchanging semi-structured data, a common practice in data integration.

Linear Poisson regression models are commonly used in time series analysis, but these models may be limited when trying to capture complex relationships between predictors and response variables. To better fit real-world data, there's a need for more flexible predictors that can adapt to changing data patterns over time. This study combines various predictor options, including time-varying, spline-based, and autoregressive splines, into a TPARM model. The proposed TPARM model demonstrates superior performance when applied to real-world datasets, outperforming existing models in terms of forecasting accuracy and model selection criteria.

This work introduces Neural Description Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that overcomes limitations of current point-based methods like PointNet and PointNet++, which suffer from high memory usage in multi-object scenarios. NDFs partition 3D space into functional regions using three equivalent points per voxel, enabling more efficient representation and reducing memory usage significantly. We demonstrate effective manipulation of NDFs for task-oriented tasks such as object classification and novel view synthesis with minimal parameters. We further show that network outputs can be directly employed to reconstruct 3D shape via Marching Cubes, bypassing the need for two-stage training and refinement. We achieve state-of-the-art performance on ModelNet40 for single-view classification and novel view synthesis, and competitive results on ShapeNet for novel view synthesis.

The precise placement of the Yang-Lee point within the O(N) universality framework has never been fully achieved globally. Utilizing the concept of the pseudo-Hermitian norm and employing both numerical functional renormalization group and Monte Carlo simulations, we have calculated this position with high accuracy across 3D and 2+1D scenarios for various values of N. Our findings reveal that the Yang-Lee point universally marks a distinct, first-order phase transition point in all O(N) models in 3D, while it represents the critical point in 2+1D scenarios with a Yang-Lee universal critical exponent framework. Unexpectedly, we have identified previously unknown values for the N-fractional parameters N+(O(-.02)) and N-(O(-.02)) in 3D, as well as N+(O(-.001)) and N-(O(-.001)) in 2+1D scenarios, in the limits of large-N.

In statistics and machine learning, basic concepts like entropy and free energy often have complicated, non-trivial properties that hold only within specific, localized areas. These properties are essential in various applications but are notoriously difficult to demonstrate theoretically. Building on an existing technique from physics known as Ampertum's rotation formula, we developed a tool called the (generalized) quenching comparison lemma that enables more straightforward demonstrations of local convexity or concavity in diverse scenarios. As practical applications of this approach, we were able to create alternative, simpler proofs for the local convexity of the TAP free energy in certain spin glass models, the concavity of the posterior free energy in Bayesian inference and variable selection, and the relationship between the expected TAP free energy and the Kullback-Leibler divergence in mean-field spin models, all of which are significant to their respective fields.

Recent modifications to the standard far-ray approximation in astronomical photometry have been addressed. 
A revised model has been developed incorporating a near-ray component and adjusted color indices to improve accuracy in astronomical measurements. 
The impact of aerosols situated between the astronomical source and the observer on photometric color indices has been examined. 
By applying a revised aerometary photometry framework to these results, aerosos parameters such as effective radius and optical depth can be derived from changes in observed color indices to nearly ray-leakage levels accurate to around the 10th decimal point. 
The near-ray component leverages nearby star comparisons, near-ray spectral emission measurements, or near-ray leakege detections, 
and utilizes a exponential law to establish a direct correlation between optical depth and ray-leakage radius. 
This developed framework offers significant improvements over existing photometric methods for astronomical aerosol assessments.

To simplify the complexities of human pose estimation, active learning is becoming increasingly essential to filter out unrepresentative data and concentrate on a narrowed set of meaningful information. By leveraging the human's innate ability to communicate and by employing correspondence-based methods, researchers have successfully reduced the dimensions of classification and segmentation problems. Building on this approach, we are set to release an enhanced version of our previous project, known as DeepHMap, called DeepHMap++, which integrates six degrees of freedom (Full DoF) pose determination for a virtual agent observing a standing person in a 2D image. Unlike conventional models, DeepHMap++ can accurately predict the agent's view of the scene and locate the person being observed, allowing it to generalize to new scenarios with ease. Through extensive experiments conducted on the COCO dataset, our model outperforms the state-of-the-art in pose estimation, segmenting, and localization, while also exhibiting an efficient and versatile architecture that paves the way for further research in this domain.

Python has seen significant growth as a data analysis and visualization tool, with
numerous established libraries available for statistical tasks such as linear
regression, classification, and probability analysis.  One key technique in this
category is GGLasso, which estimates sparse dependency graphs in data and is
implemented in R packages like GGLasso and FastGGLasso.  This paper presents a step
by step guide to developing Generalized GGLasso functionality in Python from the
ground up, and introduces an enhanced, optimized Python version of these
algorithms.  We also provide a fully functional, efficient Python version of
Generalized GGLasso along with the corresponding methodological steps.

A leading approach in statistical physics, molecular dynamics (Langevin Dynamics in this case), simulates the movement of a system's components by accounting for friction, random movement, and forces between components, which can be complex. Despite its computational intensity, it has become a common method for exploring the equilibrium arrangements of a system's components, especially in complex scenarios where other methods fail. This study presents multiple, robust enhancements to the standard Lagange Dynamics approach, including the incorporation of periodic boundary conditions, the addition of components outside the simulation box, and the management of complex interactions between components, even those extending over long distances. Our modified algorithm has been implemented in a publicly accessible Python tool, lddpy, which can be utilized to generate the equilibrium configurations of a system's components, including those with intricate interaction patterns, and produces the desired results within the specified simulation box, suitable for various analytical and experimental studies.

As multilayer networks grow increasingly prevalent, traditional promotion methods need adaptation to account for interlayer connections. While existing promotion vectors have been effective, they fall short for networks with dependent nodes. Our study introduces a novel concept of node significance across network layers and develops a new promotion measure, called reliant eigenvector, based on this concept. The result is tailored to multilayer networks and provides more accurate component promotions when tested against standard methods like eigenvector centrality and PromFAC.

While it is commonly known that the product of gamma matrices in any spacetime yields the metric tensor, there are other possible expressions with the same property. A notable example is Theorem 1, which states that in $R$-Minkowski spacetimes, the following equality holds:
$$
  \frac{1}{3!}\bigl\{\bigl[\gamma^a,\gamma^b\bigr],\gamma^c\bigr\}+\frac{1}{2}\bigl\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\gamma^c\bigr\}\gamma_a
  = \eta^{bc}\gamma^a+\eta^{ac}\gamma^b+\eta^{ab}\gamma^c,
$$
This expression provides an alternative way to derive the Minkowski metric and can be seen as an $sp(3,\mathbb{R})$-invariant form of Dirac's formula.

The process of LESS in liquids has significant implications for industrial applications and is also linked to phenomena like cavitation and jet formation. This study focuses on the  liquid entry surface seal behavior of spheres approaching a flat liquid surface, and we have analyzed and documented it in detail. A key aspect of our research involved examining the process of LESS for a range of spheres, from rigid to elastic surfaces and for surface speeds as low as 0.05 m/s. For the first time, we have documented the presence of multiple seal regimes and have established that the onset of jet formation can be predicted based on a specific criterion. We have also explored the surface velocity threshold required to induce the formation of a jet and found that for slower surface approaches, the presence of elastic surfaces promotes jet formation, whereas for faster approaches, rigid surfaces are more likely to form a jet.

In the context of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=1$ supergravity effective field theories with generic matter content, an analysis is performed on possible symmetries that cannot be achieved through field redefinitions, particularly in relation to the breaking of the shift symmetry associated with the axion-dilaton field and the exploration of extended $\theta$-like terms, including the famous "black hole" term $R\tilde{R}$, which play a crucial role in determining the feasibility of various phenomenological models, especially those involving inflation. A study of gauge group embeddings is then undertaken to illustrate some no-go results for universally breaking the axion's shift symmetry and for generating an effective $\alpha'$- or $w$-suppressed Chern-Simons interaction or an effective black hole term, respectively. A notable exception to this is when the gauge group is trivial, in which case an example is provided featuring an exponentially suppressed barrier potential and no suppression for the black hole term, which could potentially lead to gauge fields radiating enormous amounts of energy and entropy, possibly influencing the cosmic background of black holes.

Our theoretical investigation using first-principles approach and DMFT reveals orbital instability in copper-iron sulfide CuFe2S3, culminating in a rare state where electrons experience free movement along specific crystallographic bonds and localized imprisonment in others.  This phenomenon is attributed to variations in electron-sulfide interaction and results in a unusual electronic configuration, leading to semimetallic behavior and potentially explaining the material's distinct electrical conduction through pathways.  As a result, cubanite may exhibit minimal to no热电 effect.

The interstitial dark excitons in silicon exhibit massive Rabi oscillations during a resonant two-photon ionization process carried out with a microwave field, despite the photons being transversely polarized and the Rabi frequency scaling linearly with the strength of the microwave field. This phenomenon is investigated using a Hamiltonian that includes a spin-dependent dipole operator, and our findings, presented in the form of numerical and analytical results, aim to provide insight into the observed behavior. Notably, our approach allows for the estimation of the two-photon absorption cross-section for these specific dark states.

Three-dimensional lattices lack four or five-fold symmetries due to geometric constraints, which leads to two-dimensional lattices having access to all possible symmetries. In the pursuit of realizing five-fold symmetries, conventional methods require arranging non-similar polygons or shifting atoms from high-symmetry positions. However, recent discoveries show that identical lattices can maintain high symmetries without breaking, if they possess non-symmorphic elements that allow multiple sets of identical particles to exist. Although promising, utilizing such categories to host multiple quantum critical points remains unexplored. By applying this approach to a five-fold symmetric pentagonal lattice, a Mo-based pentagonal nano-mesh nanoscroll, and a double-layered pentagonal nano-mesh nanotube, all exhibit spinless Haldane models with distinct non-symmorphic symmetries and exhibit nanomesh nanoscroll and nanotube configurations with isolated nanomesh nanoscroll and nanotube structures.

Quantum catalysis, which relies on lossless intermediaries to facilitate direct particle reactions, can be utilized to generate a specific single-photon state that exhibits exhibit coherent superposition between adjacent photon number states. A four-stage setup consisting of beam splitters and a single-photon source can produce this state. Notably, a simple theoretical model based on two-stage configurations can effectively replicate the complete two-stage generation process in terms of key performance metrics. Furthermore, a comparative analysis of this single-photon state against other single-photon facilitated states reveals its capability to enhance the entanglement of a qubit formed through homodyne detection in association with an electronic auxiliary.

Using the Newman-Penrose formalism, we explore bivectors within the framework of General Relativity. We begin by establishing a Bivector field in the Newman-Penrose tetrad framework and examine its properties, including its transformation into a complex tetrad where it becomes a real algebraic special (RAS) state. We then investigate two key equations from vacuum gravity: the Newman-Penrose null tetrad formulation of RAS and the RAS form of the Einstein-Maxwell equations. Four exact solutions are presented that illustrate the RAS equations. We next define "heavy null dust" and a "bivector gravity" model. Finally, we analyze two bivector invariants and their correspondence with the squared magnitudes of the electric and magnetic Poincaré vectors of the Weyl curvature in the Newman-Penrose formalism.

This research builds upon the framework established in this thesis by exploring two key areas: first, it investigates various graph-based representations, including flow graphs, and develops corresponding deduction rules and solving algorithms, and second, it applies Monads in a comprehensive manner to represent and handle lists in Prolog, including performing arithmetic calculations on them.

Segmenting tumors in the esophagus using CT scans is still challenging due to
the low contrast of images, image artifacts, and the irregular shape of the
esophagus tumor.  In this study, we introduce a new deep learning model, called
Dilated Dense Focus Unet (DDAUnet), to improve the segmentation of the esophagus
tumors in CT scans.  Our model is based on the Dense Unet framework, with three
additional modules added: a Dense Attention Unet module, a multiple dilation
factor module, and a multiple skip connection module.  We conducted experiments
on two publicly available datasets, yielding a total Dice similarity coefficient
(DSC) score of 0.71.  Our results show that our proposed model outperforms the
Dense Unet, UNet, and three attention-based models, with an DSC score of 0.71,
compared to 0.69 for the Dense Unet, 0.67 for the UNet, 0.68 for the Skip Unet,
and 0.68 for the SE-UNet models, based on the fusion of results from two datasets.

Code-switching and code-mixing phenomena refer to the practice of integrating two or more languages by individuals, frequently within the same communication, and are prevalent in many multilingual communities globally. Although researchers have generally treated this phenomenon as interference between languages, we contend that it should be viewed as a valuable asset, offering valuable insights for developing NLP systems that cater to multilingual communities. However, such a task is not without its challenges, and we contend that current code-switching and code-mixing research focuses primarily on unrealistic and unnecessarily complicated scenarios. We propose a more practical and straightforward definition of code-mixing that distinguable four different categories of complex phenomena, two straightforward cases, and two complicated cases, and provides the associated code-mixing NLP tasks' feasible and infeasible directions.

As multiple human-to-human description generation systems are readily available, human reference information can be utilized to improve and evaluate automatic image description generation. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of this utilization remains unexplored due to the absence of guidelines on how best to apply these information. This study systematically evaluates the utility of human reference information by conducting descriptions generation both without and with this information, then compares the outcomes to establish its value. Furthermore, several critical aspects of using human reference information are investigated, including the impact of descriptions without generation augmentation versus generation augmentation on description quality, and the importance of content of these descriptions in comparison to syntax only. Additionally, simple classification models are developed to predict description quality to provide baseline performance and facilitate further research on this topic.

Tantalum oxide displays multiple distinct forms, with particular interest in a unique insulating state that occurs with five times oxidation of tantulum. To understand this unusual state, we look to a crystal structure containing formula Ta2O5, which exhibits nine different patterns. Looking at the partially filled d-band of tantalum contributes to this unusual insulating state. Of interest are two oxide phases exhibiting similar structural patterns, with Ta2O5 and NaTaO3, in which the latter exhibits ferrotatic order. To investigate the origin of this low-symmetry pattern, we turn to results predicting that even minor deviations in tantalum positioning trigger large increases in tantalum-tantalum charge separation and symmetry breaking, in turn leading to the low-symmetry phase through mechanism involving spin-orbit coupling and electron-hole transfer to O 2p holes. This dynamic process is akin to order-by-disorder phenomenon triggered by thermal or quantum fluctuations, with our study replicating thermal fluctuations via Monte Carlo simulations using thermal displacements of tantalum, in turn yielding the predicted low-symmetry phase with resulting stability margin of 10 meV per Ta2O5 unit. Of note is the emergence of ferrotatic order along with small amount of Na+ like cationic character and creation of O 2p holes leading to thermal energy scale of ~0.5 eV.

The effectiveness of geographic information visualization in promoting misinformation has been debated. This paper investigates the effectiveness of incorporating geography into misinformation dissemination strategies among users on Reddit in the United States. Our methodology involved a customized approach to extract geographic information from online messages, coupled with statistical analysis. The results indicate that large-scale geographic information significantly increases the likelihood of misinformation being spread on Reddit. In contrast, its impact varies depending on the size of the target audience's online reach. Our findings emphasize the importance of considering geographic factors in understanding and countering misinformation. They also have practical implications for improving the accuracy of predictive models for misinformation spread and the design of targeted interventions to disrupt its propagation.

Verbal guidance from human instructors plays a significant role in the efficient integration of manipulation systems. This study aims to break down and analyze these verbal instructions to enhance this integration process. Using a set of 20 instructions, we employed unit selection to assemble listening tests and gathered feedback from participants who were asked to identify the appropriate instructions for specific ongoing activities. Based on the results and our own experience, we established a new framework for categorizing acoustic patterns and found that the content and timing of when listeners were asked to detect instructions had an impact on the accuracy of their performance. This found evidence in both human participants and confirmed our hypotheses. Additionally, the assembled listening tests can be utilized to train artificial intelligence systems. Our participants were human subjects.

The fundamental concept of field theory intricate extensions was established by creating equations that represent intricate nameplate equivalences. This approach began with the Euler-Arnold equations, which, due to their established role in describing the dynamics of homogeneous fluids, have long been recognized. As early as 1920, L. Onken discovered that these equations represent an intricate identity derived from a broader equation describing the dynamics of elastic fluids. The intricate nature of this relationship has historically been challenging to explain from a geometric standpoint, primarily because the elasticity tensor's complex structure has been regarded as an enigmatic component with little physical significance. The primary objective of this study was unattainable until now: demonstrating that this intricate connection arises from an inherently geometric property. This discovery further led to a surprising interpretation of elasticity tensor's role. Additionally, the geometric framework developed in this research was applied to derive an elastic fluid model's equations, which had previously been described using ad hoc assumptions. The innovative geometric approach also prompted an explicit, though historically unappreciated, comparison with the structure of general relativity.

To enhance the functional quality of conversational systems, our proposed framework provides an efficient method for assessing the capabilities of bots through the generation of dynamic, human-like interactions. These interactions are customized to the specific areas of expertise of the bots under examination, thereby overcoming several limitations of existing evaluation methods. We illustrate our approach using a conventional conversational router as a case study, showcasing how exams can be efficiently automated. Our proposed framework incorporates the generation of structured interactions, capable of guiding bots through deliberate, content-rich conversations. Furthermore, we demonstrate the ability to incorporate domain-specific knowledge into conversational frameworks, leveraging established techniques from computer-assisted instruction. By integrating our framework with the Common Interactive Teaching format and the Open-ended Teaching Protocol, we establish the ability toassess bots in specialized fields of knowledge.

Recent years have seen the rapid expansion of e-commerce platforms, coupled
with an surge in the number of items available and customers' browsing habits,
leading to increased difficulty in locating desired items and decreased browsing
efficiency. To address this issue, cooperative recommendation systems have
become widely adopted. Nevertheless, traditional recommendation approaches rely
heavily on historical data from a single domain, limiting the scope of
knowledge that can be transferred across different domains. In response, we
propose a novel multi-domain aspect-based recommendation framework called
Multi-Sparse-Domain Aspect Preference Learning Through Comprehensive Knowledge
Transfer (MSDAP). This model incorporates a neural network-based single-domain
component and several simple-domain aspect-based components, linked by a
knowledge transfer mechanism called dual-gating. Specifically, the neural
network-like main domain component learns intricate user preferences through
historical data from one domain, while the simple-domain aspect-based
components acquire user aspect information from sparse data in other domains,
and the dual-gating technique facilitates knowledge transfer between them. The
MSDAP model achieves a breakthrough in several areas, including effective
transfer of user aspect information across multiple domains, reduced need for
training data in each domain, and better generalization capabilities. The
efficacy of the proposed model has been validated through extensive
experiments, demonstrating its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art
baselines.

Previous work by theoretical researchers demonstrated the existence of smooth, locally convex functions that approximate the behavior of convex optimization methods during iterations, although these existence proofs were non-constructive. In this study, we employ the Hypatia.jl package to derive explicit local convex quadratic models of such iterative processes in the context of linear programming, the simplex method for linear programming, and form feasibility problems with $l_1$ concave formulation. These approximations allow us to identify regions where iterative patterns are legitimately convex-like, and we've even been able to determine specific, albeit intricate, domains that define the domains of our approximations.

Medical imaging, including MRI, is extensively utilized in neurology research and clinical practice for brain imaging.
Quality assurance checks, like those performed by MRI QA phantoms, are critical to ensure images are properly acquired.
These QA phantoms, including the cerebral MRI QA, are designed to produce images in a manner that closely resemble actual patient scans.
Since the cerebral MRI QA consists of a single sample, it is indistinguishable from a generalization problem.
This paper addresses the cerebral QA phase's data limitation by applying a variety of techniques, including generative adversarial networks and transfer learning, to enhance the synthetic image's realism.
Our research demonstrates that a straightforward generative model can significantly enhance the fidelity of the cerebral MRI QA synthetic images, based on multiple evaluation metrics.

Private cars play a key role in making distribution networks more resistant to disruptions caused by external factors. To encourage the shared use of private cars and improve network resilience, there's a need for a cooperative framework that considers the private cars' own interests. Such a framework would involve both external and internal threats to the network.

In this study, we tackle the challenge of multi-agent recurrent encounters involving a large number of agents with memory capabilities. Agents in this context make decisions at each time step to either engage with another agent in the current scenario or recall past experiences to guide their actions. To guide our analysis, we introduce a fundamental problem instance called a multi-agent recurrent meeting (RAM) featuring incentive-driven behavior. To test the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct experiments using a specific class of problems, known as two-vehicle mutual rendezvous (2VR), as a baseline comparison, along with another variant that requires the vehicles to remember past locations (2VR-M). Additionally, we compare our results with those from a prevailing recurrent strategy called the multi-agent recurrent rendezvous (MARR). To evaluate the ability of agents to remember past encounters and locations, we employ a biologically-inspired incentive mechanism that targets sustained remembering behavior. To summarize, our main contributions consist of a comprehensive review of memory utilization in multi-agent settings, the development of the RAM problem, and the demonstration of the proposed incentive mechanism's effectiveness in facilitating two-agent meetings, as evidenced by experimental results.

This paper explores the structural, magnetic and electronic properties of GdSn3, CmSn3 and a series of Gd-CmSn3 alloys (Gd0.5Cm0.5Sn3, Gd0.2Cm0.8Sn3, Gd0.8Cm0.2Sn3) with a cubic Do6 structure. We examined the effect of 5.9 eV spontaneous contraction of the 6s orbitals on the crystal lattice, magnetic moments and Fermi surface topology of these compounds. Our calculations reveal that GdSn3 and its alloys display an antiferromagnetic ground state within the LMTO-ASA formalism. Notably, GdSn3 exhibits an unusual paramagnetic behavior at room temperature despite its antiferromagnetic ground state. We found that the 5.9 s-state bohr-radius contraction results in a robust 0.0045 $\mu_B$ magnetic moment on the Gd atom, unaffected by Sn interactions or alloying. Our findings also show that all Gd-CmSn3 alloys display an indium-like behavior with a 50% reduction in carrier concentration compared to GdPb3-type alloys.

This forecast paper examines the extra baryons and mesons that may exist beyond the visible matter, which has a well-determined energy density from cosmological observations. By looking into various theoretical frameworks, we explore potential candidates for these hadrons and estimate their possible abundances based on early universe conditions. It is predicted that the energy densities of these hadrons, such as neutrons, protons, and mesons, would have reached thermal equilibrium in the high-temperature conditions of the early universe. However, without adequate mechanisms to establish this equilibrium, the expected abundance of these particles would have dropped significantly as the universe expanded. Consequently, the energy densities of these hadrons would have contributed negligibly to the radiation density of the universe, consistent with observational evidence.

For any finite dimensional real vector space, we develop a geometric approach to establish a modified foundation theorem for ordered structures in $W$-posets of nonnegressive matrices. This approach utilizes the concept of W-simplices, which are defined based on a specific group of transformations that operate on the set of nonnegative matrices. As a result, we derive a modified foundation theorem for this group of transformations, extending previous findings for the special case where $\Delta = \mathbb{R}_+^l$ and drawing parallels to established theorems for convex cones and ordered structures.

The impact of supernovae type Ia lensing on the observed distribution of lensing convergence has been a subject of research for a long time, with theories and simulations suggesting that gravitational lensing can be a valuable tool for investigating dark matter within our galaxy and extragalactic populations. However, most previous studies focused solely on strongly lensed supernovae, neglecting the subtle lensing effects that are prevalent in the cosmological regime. In this study, we analyze the Pantheon sample of Type Ia supernovae to detect lensing effects by calculating the probability distributions of lensing convergence based on the observed $m_{\rm{obs}}-\alpha_{\rm{obs}}$ color-magnitude parameters. We also examine the impact of variable source and lens ellipticities on the observed parameters, finding that lens ellipticities can introduce asymmetries in the $m_{\rm{obs}}-\alpha_{\rm{obs}}$ distribution that can be used as a method for detecting dark matter around galaxies. Utilizing the PANORAMA N-body simulation, we identify a 2.4 sigma level of significance in the presence of lensing effects by filtering the data based on the redshift of the lensed supernovae.

A new class of photonic structures, known as T-shaped resonators, has been developed to enhance the functionality of integrated optical systems. These T-shaped structures have been modeled using two-dimensional and three-dimensional methods, and their characteristics have been compared to those of U-shaped resonators. Through experimentation, it has been discovered that T-shaped resonators offer distinct advantages over U-shaped alternatives, providing greater flexibility in application while maintaining similar performance levels. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that T-shaped structures can be utilized to develop a photonic ring resonator array with an innovative T-junction coupling scheme, which offers a wider range of applications than traditional straight-waveguide based systems.

Deep learning-based object detection models leverage contextual information to enhance their performance in object localization and classification. To further exploit this contextual advantage, we developed context-aware object detectors by integrating feature fusion-based methods that utilize background information. Our approach, however, reveals that for highly nonlinear objects like vehicles, the background can introduce significant confusion, hindering the effectiveness of our context-aware detector. To overcome this challenge, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the object and background foreground+ and - and the surrounding context, +, -. Based on this investigation, we established four distinct scenes: object-only, background-only, mixed, and contextual, +, -. Our research signifies the first systematic examination of context objects-, background+/- in the realm of deeper object detection models. To sum up, our context-aware object detector leverages different processing methods by utilizing the unique characteristics of each scene. Our experimental outcomes demonstrate that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art in object detection for objects deeply embedded within their environments.

We consider a Kirchhoff type elliptic equation with a nonlocal coefficient, a measure singular term and a growth term of a exponential type over a bounded domain in R2. By using rearrangements and comparison arguments we are interested in proving a combination result with respect to the set of measures that not positive functions can occupy. A nonlocal change of variables and an oscillating test function allow us to obtain qualitative existence outcomes for nondegenerate and degenerate inhomogeneous equations. Furthermore, by incorporating exponential decay factors without loss of generality, we are able to obtain existence conclusions for inhomogeneous Kirchhoff type equations that previously did not exist.

The well known concentration phenomenon for sums of independent random 
variables has been extensively investigated. In this work, we examine the 
impact of mild dependence, specifically short-range negative correlation, on 
concentration properties. We derive comparable concentration properties for 
sums under mild negative correlation, demonstrating the resilience of this 
property in that context.

Luxemburg recently introduced the concept of symplectic modification to partially ordered sets, which generalizes the Partial Blowing up operation. In this paper, we introduce a broader definition of "symplectic modification" that encompasses both our process and Luxemburg's original definition. Using this framework, we prove that any two symplectic versions of a poset are isomorphic to one another, establishing the fact that such transformations preserve the combinatorial structure of a poset up to equivalence.

Transplanting kidneys that are incompatible with the recipient can significantly shorten waiting times and save lives, yet it is not widely performed due to medical and societal resistance.  To investigate what influences people's willingness to accept such kidneys, we conducted interviews with 40 volunteers in the US and Italy, comprising healthcare professionals, technologists, and the general public.  Our discussions included individuals who had experienced kidney transplants, physicians, and members of the public, focusing on medically incompatible kidneys.  Using the method of conversational exchanges guided by the principle of conversational cooperation, we found that willingness to accept incompatible kidneys varies among individuals and is influenced by personal experiences, trust in medical professionals, and perceptions of the transplants' success rates.  Our findings can assist in developing educational materials and improving public communication regarding organ transplantation.

This study scrutinizes whether words from eight pre-trained linguistic embedding models can accurately categorize companies based on their financial statements, aligning with a well-known financial database, Loughran-McDonald's sentiment dictionary.

Our empirical findings diverge from prior conclusions drawn in non-financial contexts, indicating that seven of the eight embedding models fail to distinguish between highly positive and negatively framed companies. Furthermore, we discovered that only seven out of 50,000 companies from the year 2010 exhibited extremely positive or negative sentiments, and the models consistently flagged certain companies with anomalous sentiment scores, misclassifying them with overwhelmingly high probabilities.

Our research also explored the underlying causes of these misclassifications and established correlations between the embeddings' performance and specific factors. Notably, we found that seven of the models' textual representations captured chronological patterns but struggled to differentiate between positive and negative sentiments within the Loughran-McDonald polarity database.

This work presents modified waveforming techniques for broadband integrated data and power transfer (IDPT) systems with single or single-antenna send/receive components, addressing potential equivalence issues that arise in SISO-IDPT and MISO-IDPT configurations. Potential obstacles to achieving configuration equivalence are circumvented, enabling maximum gain from multiple antennas and multiple carriers to be achieved by optimizing only two parameters: the power allocation vector and the precoder for power signals, regardless of the IDPT system configuration. The proposed modifications allow for the development of efficient training and signal processing schemes by establishing relationships between broadband IDPT configuration equivalents, specifically BIDPT-equivalent OFDM (BOIDPT and MOIDPT) and time-domain IDPT (TIDPT) equivalents. The concept of broadband IDPT equivalents is then applied to OFDM and single-carrier IDPT techniques, providing a unified framework for analyzing multiple antennas and carrier configurations in integrated systems.

This research examines the growth of solidification and growth of molten pools on a rotating platform, taking into account the Coriolis force. The orientation of the axis of rotation can be horizontal or tilted in relation to the interface between the molten pool and a solid interface. This setting is highly relevant to the growth of moons within gas giants like Jupiter. We've conducted numerical simulations using an embedded boundary technique to handle such problems, where the research includes both 2D and moving interface 3D scenarios. A rotating coordinate technique has been employed to switch over while minimizing grid distortion in the latter case. Furthermore, a method has been developed to combine different levels of embedded boundary techniques, enabling accurate and efficient handling of interface distortions in 3D. Our technique has been shown to successfully capture the interface distortions in both 2D and 3D cases with little distortion of the computational grid.

We investigate learning outcomes that fall within the framework of rationalizability in multiplayer games featuring continuously changing rewards. By employing the standard external update rule with typical learning methods, we show that the average payoff converges to the set of rationalizable equilibria for both a two-player game and an n-player competition in an infinite time frame. Furthermore, in the n-player case, the projected velocities of the payoff updates of all players also converge to the average payoffs as time goes on.

A significant issue with virus outbreaks is how rapidly they spread. If individuals who become infected can't be instantly quarantined, the spread of the disease might continue unchecked. This research introduces a new concept of epidemic resistance by allowing infected people to break links in their social network and form new connections with unknown individuals. By constantly changing their connections, infected people increase the chance of the virus's propagation path forming a closed loop, effectively containing the outbreak's spread. Our findings reveal that this strategy can substantially slow down or even prevent the widespread transmission of the disease, providing a surprising benefit of rewiring in contaminated social settings.

This paper proposes a systematic method for PDF modification, extending the work of Keimer et al. (2016). Our approach represents changes as shifts in structure and probability, bypassing the direct effect on observed distributions. This is particularly relevant for modern particle physics research, where experiments focus on specific final states rather than specific particles. By focusing on final states, our framework is meaningful for the refinement of particle data tables. We further expand our framework to incorporate shifts in hadron structure due to reference frame variations, and discuss the impact of this on the available particle data tables.

Reinforcement learning algorithms often incorporate experience replay to boost both their performance and ability to generalize by allowing them to learn from past experiences. However, standard experience replay lacks a variance reduction mechanism, making it similar to i.i.d sampling, which has a limited sample efficiency. We introduce a new method called Policy Based Experience Replay (PBER), which reduces the variance and expands the replay pool by dynamically adjusting the probability of revisiting past experiences based on an agent's current policy. We also develop a variant of PBER known as Simple PBER with simplified policy probabilities to accommodate current limitations in large-scale policy spaces. We evaluate PBER and Simple PBER against the standard experience replay method across multiple policy-learning frameworks, consistently observing improved performance in various settings.

In order to handle complex, multi-way conversations where conversations continue across different directions simultaneously, our study presents the MultiTalk challenge, achice for ambitious, multi-way dialogue management.  Currently, most dialogue systems only handle simple, one-on-one conversations, which are too simple to reflect real-world, simultaneously occurring conversations. The key components of the generated dataset, which consists of over 150,000 conversation snippets, are outlined in order to facilitate the creation of the data for the challenge. A strategy for gathering data is presented which outlines three methods for collecting data for single-agent, multi-agent, and continuous conversations. To support the development of the MultiTalk dataset, we describe the context, topics, and structure of the data used. Additionally, we provide guidelines for creating annotations that outline five strategies for generating labels. To support the development of models for the MultiTalk challenge, we present several baseline approaches, including a random reply generator and two existing one-on-one conversation models. The discussion section delves into the difficulties posed by multi-way dialogue and discusses possible directions for future research.

Researchers are expanding their knowledge of gravity by altering general relativity, with cosmological studies being a key area of development. To facilitate these studies, simulations based on N-body calculations for large-scale structure formation are crucial. However, the complexity of most modified gravity theories requires rigorous simulations, which are time-consuming and limit the scope of parameter space that can be explored. To overcome this limitation, we developed a set of N-body simulations for the tensor scalar linking (tsl) model, a representative of modified gravity theories, using the guc code. Our focus was on expanding the studies of modified gravity models by producing large simulations to accurately structure formation. By linking only at linear level, our model achieves significant reductions in computation time while maintaining the ability to reproduce key features of full N-body simulations. Our full results for structure formation for various choices of parameters in the tensor and scalar sectors are available for a broad range of application to models that have been linked in a conformal way, thus allowing the efficient exploration of a multidimensional parameter space.

Building on Schramm's theory of multiple stochastic Loewner evolution, we examine the connections between the growth of $n$ interacting curves and the behavior of a two-dimensional Brownian motion within the resulting complex domains. Bases for recent research in this field, particularly related to the work of Lawler, Miller, Peres, and Virag, as well as the author's own studies, are provided. We demonstrate the equivalence of two distinct characterizations of the Gaussian free field. Additionally, we provide a second method for generating multiple SLE curves using a random log-gas. Notably, when $n=2$ and the driving force of the random log-gas is sufficiently large, we show that the complex domain formed by the SLE curves is hyperbolic.

In scientific disciplines, collaborative projects involving multiple collaborators are becoming increasingly common.
For projects with a large number of collaborators, the level of communication required can be daunting.
To effectively work together, the team behind WorkingWiki developed a cooperative workflow and documentation system based on MediaWiki.
We believe that this approach, along with our customized "WorkingWiki" platform, facilitates effective knowledge sharing among participants in complex, interdisciplinary projects.
Here, we describe the structure and media wiki-based workflow of our platform in detail, while sharing our experiences and lessons learned from using it in a high-level, interdisciplinary project.
Additionally, we provide the source code for our platform to enable its application in other high-level projects.

This research reaction to a jet fire within a linear system framework, where it modeled how a flame's fluctuation caused variations in heat output, resulting in structural damage or deformation. To achieve non-linear outcomes, the AJFM was used to apply intense thermal variation to a specific area of a model, causing areas of stress failure that matched the expected non-linear behavior. By comparing simulations both with and without flame variation, the necessity for an accurate thermal source to reach the stress threshold was established. The study also determined the extent of the stress threshold and identified the factors influencing the AJFM's effectiveness, including the type of fuel, the level of excitation, the excitation frequency, the level of damping, and the structural material's thickness, all while maintaining the same dimensions of the model and source, both numerically and experimentally.

The investigation of neutrino mass through the $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay neeuds of chargeless leptons and from extreme astronomical objects like neutron stars is reviewed. Within the framework where the ultralight dark matter exists as coherent classical waves with a specific wavelength and frequency, the $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay neeuds get a distinct, but minor, boost in the duration of a typical nuclear decay process. In the context of neutron stars, the possibility of the decay process $n \to p + e^-$ gaining energy from the ultralight dark matter leads to an increase in the neutrino flux emerging from neutron stars that might be detectable by neutrinoless double beta decay experiments involving Earth-based neutrons. The rate of this process also opens up the potential for the partial conversion of neutrons into protons within a neutron star, which could result in an abrupt, explosive event that produces high-energy neutrinos and potentially observable gravitational waves.

This research examines a reformulated gravity theory known as nonlocal gravitation, which has been developed based on general relivation. In this new framework, two distinct components are introduced to describe the relationship between nonphysical variables called tetrads and physically meaningful connections in a manifold. These components, called constitutive connections, are described as functions of tetrads and directly influence a specific type of field equation. These equations can be used to solve for essential tetrads when paired with a specific type of field equation called the Bianchi identity. This process results in a precise reconstruction of the field equations of general relivation, including the correct energy and momentum conservation laws. We have demonstrated that the nonlocal gravitation framework is not unique and can be expanded to yield various field equations that accurately represent general relivation. This includes a specific type of gravitation theory called Poincaré gauge theory, which differs in its approach but achieves the same physical results.

This study aims to explore and improve two methods for analyzing genomic data on quantitative traits, considering three potential associations between genes and genes that may skew traditional models and conducting a detailed examination of association studies for eight human traits across researchers from various institutions. By utilizing information from gene functions, we identify and address three potential associations between genes and genes, and through meta-analysis and comparative examination of ten traits including alcohol preference, we collaborate to further study genome-wide association studies in humans.

Inquiries into tiny systems produced in lead-lead collisions at the LHC have a high significance, given that they offer invaluable information to interpret pp data. Due to the limited availability of PP data, our understanding of specific inelastic processes and parton distribution functions for low-x quarks and gluons remains restricted. As a result, simulations based on QCD require input from both quark and gluino processes to accurately predict the outcome of Pb-Pb data. Hence, the production of tiny systems based on pp collisions is crucial to understand the first step towards heavy ion physics. Based on the latest findings from Pb-Pb and Pb-p collisions at $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}= 5.02$ TeV, we discover that tiny systems produced in Pb-Pb collisions are highly saturated, indicating their close resemblance to the initial state of heavy ion physics.

Observations of the universe have revealed numerous examples of accreting objects in our galaxy and beyond repeatedly feeding on particular parts of their surroundings. In many instances, these objects release enormous amounts of energy during repeated outbursts that are remarkably similar in duration and frequency. This study focuses particularly on neutron star systems in our galaxy that are currently inactive and investigates possible underlying mechanisms that could explain the repetitive patterns in the-fueller of these systems, which often remain hidden in the dark regions of the Milky Way. Although some possible explanations exist, no evidence has been found thus far for this phenomenon in observations. However, some theoretical models suggest that certain patterns of repetition may be intrinsic to these systems and predicts that a set of typical intervals between outbursts of these systems would be concentrated within a specific range in our galaxy. These predictions are mostly in line with a variety of data obtained from recent surveys of inactive X-ray binaries in the centre of our galaxy that show a prominent repetition period of 10 to 100 years on top of a variety of different repetition intervals.

Momentum fluctuations in a quantum system are shown to give rise to new types of non-adiabatic effects, resulting in "momentum-induced" non-collinearity between spins and nuclear momenta, as well as the breakdown of the Born-Oppenheimer approximation between electrons and nuclei. Unlike other non-adiabatic phenomena, these effects do not require small parameters such as mass ratios or perturbation parameters to occur, and are instead universally significant. This has broad implications for various fields of study, as the associated cross-coupling terms do not decay and cannot be ignored on either the vibrational or electronic energy scales.

In our Natural Language Inference (NLI) model for Natural Dialogue, we naturalize the task by incorporating three key elements: the interplay of natural language statements and background discourse, the presence of implicit needs, and semantic variability due to its conversational nature. We source background discourse and implicit needs from real, multi-turn conversations that lack an explicit target statement, and we embrace the vocabulary and phraseology variability inherent to such discussions.

Recent discoveries of direct photons and neutrinos from coherent processes require the existence of rotating sub-stellar objects like boson stars, and potentially MAE stars. To understand these signals, a numerical model was developed for the boundary conditions of rotating sub-stellar objects, and 1D numerical simulations were conducted using effective field theory and the Einstein-equations. The simulations reveal that the rotation threshold behaves differently for massive and massless particles, and that increasing the rotation speed leads to a reduction in the stars radius, culminating in the formation of black holes beyond a critical point.

Visual representations of residual errors or data residuals often incorporate representations of the actual data points, including their associated uncertainties. A common approach involves drawing lines that extend from each point, but this method can be misleading as it implies the uncertainties are linear variations. A more accurate depiction should reflect the probabilistic nature of the uncertainties, by using shapes such as parabolas or probability density curves at the ends of lines representing each point. This article demonstrates modification techniques for various plotting commands in Gnuplot, Matplotlib, and R to effectively implement this form of visualization.

Dynamical systems theory often employs phase portraits to depict the evolution of time-dependent phenomena. We adapt this concept by developing a posterior light curve equation suitable for a broad class of afterglows, encompassing various energy distributions, density distributions, and bulk motion distributions. This equation, when applied, allows us to analyze afterglows by identifying key components that contribute to the overall brightness, which can be visually represented in a "light curve space" similar to a phase portrait. When examining afterglows from GRBs, we discover that their complexity ranges from simple two-component models to more intricate multi-component models, with sources exhibiting particularly unusual light curve profiles requiring significant attention.

Given a graph G and a parameter k, our study develops an algorithm to partition the vertices of G into singletons and pairs K_2 in a way that the resulting subgraph contains no edges longer than those of the complement of the graph formed by the k-length path or cycle. Our method achieves this with an efficiency of O(2^{k^5})·n.

This project focuses on investigating the potential of propulsion-assisted bipedal locomotion in both dynamic and static scenarios. We will develop, analyze, and experimentally validate mathematical models of propulsion-assisted locomotion in both cases. In the dynamic context, our team will create and assess a lightweight, highly maneuverable bipedal robot with two versions of its legs - jamber and telescopic - to explore the propulsion-assisted locomotion methods. In the static scenario, we will apply our insights to enhance the resilience and energy efficiency of heavy-load foraging ants. By the end of the project, we aim to significantly enhance the load-to-body weight ratio carried by our bipedal robot during the static scenario and generate valuable data on the effects of propulsion-assisted locomotion in both dynamic and static situations.

Given a nonarchimedean field K and integers a_1,...,a_n that are coprime, we examine the set K_1^0 where the reduction of the first coordinate of its elements forms a complete residue map. We focus on identifying respected fields K with specific properties: the existence of a in the set of integers such that a times the product of the a_i's is coprime to the uniformizer of K, or the ability to solve the equation a times x plus the sum of the a_i's times x_i's = 1 where the x, x_i's are elements of the residue field of K. We can extend our findings to cases where the a_i's are not necessarily coprime.

To improve privacy and security, we've developed HyperDegrade, an automated framework for testing and optimizing side-channel mitigation techniques. 
Side-channel issues, where past computations impact future memory addresses, have become increasingly significant, particularly as memory virtualization methods have evolved. 
HyperDegrade, which is capable of running on current CPUs with limited time resources, consists of two primary components: a side-channel assessment tool and a mitigation evaluation template. 
The former, SideRecon, generates side-channel tests by automatically creating statistical models of past computations and identifying leaks through hypothesis testing, while the latter, MitRecon, produces side-channel-leak-sensitive programs for mitigations to handle. 
HyperDegrade's efficiency, versatility, and versatility have been demonstrated through the development and assessment of side-channel mitigations, including an evaluation of existing technologies and the creation of a novel technique, OTF, for mitigating side-channel leaks.

A specific loop within  positive octant of $\R_+^3$, known as the Fox-Hatcher loop, 
is shown to have a non-zero Vassiliev characteristic of order three, 
which implies that this loop can not be realized as the boundary of a 
volume-minimizing disk in the positive octant.

In our study, we investigate the issue of tactical multi-agent collaboration within a tactical teaming framework, building upon the foundation laid by Gilbert et al. In this approach, artificial intelligence agents operate within real-time simulated environments with limited computation and communication capabilities, making they experience information deprivation and constrained communication channels. We focus on the issue of tactical teaming, where the moral dilemmas are replaced with scenarios requiring a decision between various courses of action that have wide-ranging consequences. We employ a variant of a commonly used moral decision-making prototype and conduct experiments to assess the effectiveness of our results through performance metrics. Our data reveals that tactical teaming can be modeled using a variation of moral dilemmas and that collaborative tactics can be taught to the participants under challenging conditions.

This work examines two realistic privacy risks associated with using federated learning for education. In this educational setting, multiple institutions come together to train a model with the assistance of shared knowledge bases. While embracing the advantages of collaborative learning, it is imperative to give due consideration to the potential privacy risks associated with FPAD. Through a series of simulations, we demonstrate how various memory-based attack techniques can compromise models by reconstructing training samples. These results highlight the critical importance of employing robust privacy-assured methods to implement the promising framework of collaborative learning for education. To address these privacy concerns, we introduce a solution that combines training data encryption with countermeasures to safeguard against memory-based assaults and allows several institutions to collaborate on educational programs. Additionally, we present an alternative approach using a cryptographic protocol to counter assaults from malicious participants. Both approaches are evaluated through a series of realistic scenarios and real-world data, showing that they allow institutions to collaborate on educational programs while protecting the sensitive data of their students.

Traditional kernel estimation methods rely on fixed kernel functions, which are independent of input data. In contrast, this paper introduces a novel approach to kernel estimation that estimates a kernel function based on input data, particularly useful in the context of Universal Sample Compression Reconstructors (USCR). We propose two methods for creating pseudo-random attributes that facilitate this estimation, and demonstrate that our approach yields more accurate reconstructions than existing PPM-based techniques with minimal computational cost and memory usage, as well as enabling the use of highly complex kernel functions. Our approach is evaluated using real-world datasets, showing significant improvements in reconstruction accuracy compared to current methodologies.

This paper presents a proof that any finite group can be embedded into a product of garland spaces, denoted as $\bigtimes_{\bigtimes}G$, through a specific type of decomposition known as a Cartesian decomposition. The structure of these garland products was initially defined by Davis and Wise in 2005, and the current definition used is equivalent. The key difference lies in the ordering of the components of the product, which, in our representation, must be arranged according to the partial order of their end boundaries, denoted as $\partial_{\pm}$. The method of proving this embedding is distinct from the original boundary-based approach, employing a Cartesian decomposition instead.

We prove a conformal invariant version of Minkowski's classic $\mathbb{R}^n$ hypersurface theorem under Gauss map orientation, stating that a Mobius equivalent, properly immersed, compact conformally $\mathbb{S}^{n+1}$ hypersurface in $\mathbb{S}^{n+2}$ space must have non-decreasing average scalar curvature than $\mathbb{S}^{n+1}$ sphere under the natural ordering. Furthermore, this hypersurface has the same M\"obius scalar curvature as $\mathbb{S}^{n+1}$ sphere if and only if it's conformally equivalent to the standard sphere under the appropriate naming convention.

A new wireless system concept called multi-service SWIPT was introduced recently, allowing a single drone to share its energy-harvesting capabilities across multiple frequencies. The goal is to figure out the best way to distribute resources for maximum energy gain by the drone. This study analyzes the energy harvest from the drone using a simplified model that considers a log-normal distribution for signal phases and Rayleigh fading. It's discovered that non-energy signals have minimal impact on overall energy harvest due to their phases being uniformly distributed. Furthermore, optimal energy signals provide the most benefit when signal powers are limited, while non-energy signals' dimensions should be minimized to reduce unnecessary interference. To make things more complex in unidirectional SWIPT systems, the previously derived recommendations are no longer valid.

The concept of a Cayley graph represents the equivalence between a group and its structure, where the graph's connectivity corresponds to a generating set. When a set is randomly chosen based on a given probability distribution, it can determine a group's generation, and accordingly, Cayley graphs emerge as outcome spaces associated with a specific sampling process. Leveraging the properties of extreme values of i.i.d random variables, we establish that the distribution of generating sets on finite groups reaches an avalanche-scale, characterized by a 50% probability of generation. This phenomenon is indicative of a sudden, dramatic shift. Moreover, in the case of abelian groups, we demonstrate that this extreme random outcome aligns with the structure and symmetry of the group by showing invariance under left multiplication and a high probability of left-translation randomness. These findings are applicable and valuable for algorithmic group theory, particularly in developing an efficient sampling procedure to produce generating sets with a probability of one.

The detection sensitivity of laser interferometric gravitational wave detectors in the high-frequency range above 100Hz is受限 by the movement of mirrors. To improve responsiveness to gravitational waves in the high-frequency range, we propose proposing an novel design known as a "sloshing" Sagnac interferometer, which links two optical cavities in a specific configuration. This design ensures that a photon circulates the entire system twice, effectively isolating the internal cavities from each other from the perspective of the photon, while providing mutual compensation for the phase introduced by the input optics and minimizing the degree of freedom that influences the detector's high-frequency response. According to theoretical calculations, the sloshing configuration enables the detector to respond to the vibration of the secondary suspension of the secondary mirror at a frequency of 2.5 MHz, compared to the typical response range of 250 kHz in conventional configurations.

This report delves into an intriguing finding related to spatial access methods in extreme large-scale MIMO systems, where distinct nodes can experience identical backoff expiration times and yet remain within each other's communication range without intersecting. This counterintuitive occurrence is explored through theoretical analysis and simulation, with implications for access control in extreme large-scale MIMO environments examined. Furthermore, potential enhancements to current techniques, aimed at preventing such non-intersecting scenarios in extreme large-scale MIMO settings, are discussed.

Recent high-resolution observations of dust substructures at millimeter and submillimeter wavelengths by the ALMA telescope have become increasingly common. To better interpret these observations, theoretical models must be developed to accurately replicate them. To proceed, we created a new model that replicates gas and gas-driven dust dynamics, building upon our previous model that only accounted for gas and dust behavior. Key factors such as gas radiation, gas cooling, and two-body gravitational interactions were incorporated into this model. Notably, we found that including the vertical shear instability (VSI) and radial drift significantly impacted the distribution of dust and led to the formation of large-scale substructures observed in the continuum observations. We found that this model also replicated previous findings that didn't include the effects of radiation. When comparing this model to one that only accounted for the gravitational instability, we discovered that ripples were primarily formed by VSI and radial drift near the disk surface, while spiral arms were mainly formed by gravitational instability in the disk midplane. Since this model primarily accounted for ripples rather than spiral arms, we developed a simpler, radius-based prediction tool that could be tested against the new, more detailed model or applied directly to observe only the dust behavior. As gravitational instabilities may not form prominently in a wide range of disks observable by the ALMA telescope, the VSI and radial drift may be the key factors that form the substructures seen in the dust continuum observations.

A novel three-body force, called Big Apple, is introduced in relativistic geometry, and its impact is examined in finite nuclei as well as in astronomical objects. When applied to finite nuclei, the Big Apple force significantly enhances spin-orbit splitting and isomer energy differences. In astronomical objects such as neutron stars and magnetars, it leads to a notable increase in moment of inertia and reduces the star's tidal deformability.

This research examines the robustness of Molmer-Sorensen gates in ion traps to various levels of frequency impurity, given an equal amplitude of laser fields. In scenarios with high frequency impurity levels, we demonstrate the effectiveness of adjusting field amplitudes for each laser beam to maintain coherent states and achieve precise, synchronized pulses. Our simulations, conducted on actual data from an aluminum nitide resonator, reveal that by balancing the amounts of energy in various motion modes with a particular pulse pattern, we can significantly reduce the error of MS gates, even in the presence of high frequency impurity. We achieve a reduction in error by two orders of magnitude compared to conventional methods. Our study also provides insights into mitigating noise caused by phase fluctuations in the laser.

Using a combination of a non-equilibrium approach and first-principles methodology, we developed a framework to study time-induced Dirac solids, addressing the needs of experimenters. Through this approach, we identified four distinct phases in the t-k space of such systems, with a focus on two key components: crystal momentum and time. These phases are: parabolic semim semim, and two types of gapped insulators occurring when both natural and time-induced gaps close. The natural gap closure defines a non-essential Dirac point, whereas the simultaneous closing of both gaps results in a essential Dirac point, acting as an anchor for various topological phases. When a semi-Heisenberg semim semim and an anomalous Chern insulator are connected, a anomalous Haldane insulator appears. The topological invariants and dynamic properties of this system were investigated, and we demonstrated that a semi-CHern semim semim and an anomalous Haldane insulator can be reversibly transformed into each other. The proposed theory can be realized in a variety of systems, and we highlight c-Sn as a starting point for experimental investigation.

We are anticipating the NA62 NA62mu2 upgrade to explore neutral lepton theories by analyzing non-observed $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ decay, resulting in missing energy and transverse momentum. To simulate visible data with zero background, we created a Monte Carlo model of detector response, yielding an event sample of 4.8 million $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ decays, given 10^19 incoming $K^+$ mesons and zero background. This signal could be identified via missing mass and transverse momentum, with a proposed selection strategy yielding ~100 allowed parameter space events. Notable beyond-Standard Model explanations, such as the sterile neutrino and scalar neutrino, are discussed.

Our hypothesis that neurons in neural language models mimic $n$-gram languages was supported by experimental evidence, prompting us to utilize this discovery to enhance neural language models through the transfer of non-neural $n$-gram languages across domains. Our experiments demonstrated a significant improvement of up to 10 points in tasks involving neural text generation when residual learning with $n$-gram models was used as encoders. Additionally, this approach allowed for increased efficiency by reducing training time and computational costs by approximately four times.

The primary face reconstruction task aims to create 3D face models from images, with numerous real-world applications, particularly those relying on precise, robust, and 3D face reconstruction techniques. Current developments in this area often generate models with models that accurately replicate facial features but struggle with accurate spatial arrangement and overall face shape. The challenge is compounded by the presence of distorted and occluded faces in input images. To address this issue, we developed SADRNet, which produces self-aligned 3D face models by integrating two competing networks that learn to align and reconstruct faces. Our method incorporates an attention mechanism to capture global and local information, thereby improving the spatial accuracy and shape quality of the generated models. Our method was validated through face reconstruction, depth reconstruction, and ablation studies on publicly available 3D face images and heavily deformed and occluded datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness.

This investigation explores the use of the iOCR library for streamlining the
processing of large-scale election results. iOCR simplifies the utilization of
PaddleOCR, integrating key components that otherwise require manual processing.
PaddleOCR often misidentifies characters, leading to issues like "O" being

This approach effectively processes test datasets and is discussed in the context

In traditional econometric analysis, selecting an appropriate model is commonly assumed to be intuitive and unambiguous. However, this assumption is questionable, particularly given the frequent occurrence of "benign misfitting." This phenomenon occurs when an unnecessarily intricate true model is modeled using an under-complex linear regression, typically resulting from data limitations or model specification limitations. In most cases, benign misfitting leads to asymptotically equivalent forecast frameworks and statistical inference methods as shown through the development of an carefully simulated dataset. This study further proves the validity of standard inference procedures and forecasting methods in asymptotically relaxed settings, even when the underlying and proposed models both exhibit over-parameterization.

In this study, a cautious storage planning approach is introduced for an agent operating within a network of peers. Rather than optimizing for the collective good, the agent aims to minimize risk by using a cautious variant of the widely adopted storage management framework known as the Pooling Benchmark (PB).
