This research continues our examination of the unique behavior of molten polymers confined within irregular shapes, focusing on highly irregular shapes with elongated, molten "brush" structures. When these polymers reach a certain molecular weight threshold, a phenomenon known as "end exclusion" occurs in such irregular shapes. We developed a theoretical model to explain how polymers behave in these shapes at high molecular weights, using "star bristles" as a reference. This helped us understand that end exclusion can only happen in these shapes with multiple arms, not in shapes with a single curved surface. Additionally, using neutron scattering, we tested our findings by investigating the behavior of molten polymers in a specific highly irregular shape, known as the SDB macroscopic sphere, at both high and low molecular weights. This experiment supported the end exclusion theory, but also revealed that end exclusion does not happen in shapes with a single curved surface, as predicted. Both experimental data and simulation data matched well in this study.

A graph G is considered uniquely resolvable if a subset of its vertices can distinguish between all other vertices in the graph. The smallest subset of vertices that uniquely resolves G is known as the uniquely resolvable dimension. We are currently investigating the concepts of metrics for graphing by focusing on a newly defined parameter, the shortened metric dimension, which is based on restricted uniquely resolvable subsets of vertices that map to distinct locations in a graph of a reduced size. This paper introduces and studies the corresponding uniquely half-resolvable and uniquely third-resolvable metrics, establishing relationships with other known graph parameters, such as the half-metric dimension and the metric dimension, and providing a similarly structural characterization for the latter.

The concept of cosmic rays and gamma rays, first proposed by physicists in the 1960s, was realized with the advent of the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, launched in 2008. A significant challenge in analyzing gamma-ray data lies in its statistical limitations, particularly when examining specific areas of the sky. This challenge can be overcome by employing regression models to predict relationships between observed variables and measured emissions. Recent studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of such models in global maps, including weather patterns and ocean surface temperatures, by 2022. Building on this foundation, this research utilizes a segment of Fermi-LAT data from 2008 to 2019 to explore the application of these models in gamma-ray physics, specifically by: a) determining the nightly all-sky map predicted by learning techniques, and, b) identifying celestial objects exhibiting day-to-day variability, including: A) the Milky Way, and, B) the diffuse extragalactic background. Our analysis reveals that this approach can establish meaningful connections in gamma-ray data, with the diffuse background exhibiting the highest prediction complexity due to its higher energy levels. The models further indicate temporal trends in the all-sky map, with the diffuse background showing the most significant patterns, and objects exhibiting variability are distinguished by different spectral characteristics compared to the diffuse background.

A serial dictatorship mechanism is considered inferior to a serial dictatorship framework, which includes all possible sequential mechanisms. It has been proven that the class of welfare-maximizing frameworks for all possible sequential mechanisms can't exceed the class of welfare-maximizing individual functions. However, our research reveals that this class of frameworks exceeds that all possible simultaneous mechanisms in terms to maximizing social welfare in nearly all instances, specifically with all instances exceeding two participants and two goods and preparations to indefinitely so with any number to participants and goods. It has been also found out that our proposed class of frameworks to maximizing welfare can exist even two instances maximizing welfare with simultaneous mechanisms and all possible nodes to trees to maximizing welfare with a serial dictatorship node in each path of the tree.

We developed a straightforward technique to detect catalog entries with phase effects, aiming to identify single asteroids and distinguish them from binary ones within the Pan-STARRS1 data. This involved creating a new feature, psfelongation, based on arcfox features to analyze the movement of 432 main belt asteroids. Although our method can't confirm the binary nature of the identified target, it flags potential binary asteroids for closer examination. Our research reveals that 10 catalog entries, including 6 previously unlisted small asteroids, may exhibit signs of binary systems.

Large-scale networks provide a powerful framework for estimating complex, interdependent variables and can be employed to develop novel statistical methods for studying such relationships. This article partially outlines the connection between variable networks and statistical frameworks, focusing on semi-parametric models, specifically the partial linear framework. The practical application of network data is demonstrated by evaluating the relationship between peer influence and a variable of interest, between school attendance and peer peer lending, and between air quality and local air pollution dispersal networks. The novel connection between network data and partial linear framework is explored in more depth in Section 2.

This study explores the properties of the Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional integral and derivative, focusing on a new expression known as the Leibniz rule. A new way to apply the Riemann-Liouville fractional integral to a product of two functions is derived in this paper. The fixed expression of the Riemann-Liouville variable-order differential of the product of two functions is obtained through a caputo variable-order fractional derivative in particular cases.

Our novel approach, called ID3X, builds upon traditional LLM Dungeons and Dragons experiences by employing an AI Dungeon Supervisor that engages in D&D tabletop role-playing and leverages its enhanced reasoning capabilities to guide the game.  Unlike conventional LLM Dungeons and Dragons platforms where the game proceeds unguided, ID3X incorporates an AI Dungeon Supervisor that adapts its guidance style to accommodate the players' preferences and fosters a personalized and engaging gaming environment. To achieve this, we developed a non-invasive and adaptive method called Multi-Agent Learning with Explicit Intent (MALEINT) that enables the AI Dungeon Supervisor to communicate effectively with the players and make informed decisions regarding its role as a game moderator. Through extensive assessments involving both subjective player feedback and objective game metrics, our results indicate that ID3X successfully creates a more engaging and personalized gaming environment that is tailored to the players' preferences. Our findings also demonstrate that ID3X is capable of engaging in a cohesive and purposeful gaming experience with the players.

Knotted proteins possess intricate three-dimensional structures that defy their generally linear chemical composition. Recent chemical and biological breakthroughs have significant implications for understanding how knotted proteins form and function. While linear proteins lack three-dimensional cohesion, they are believed to adopt complex spatial configurations, potentially influencing knotting probability. Although the biological fluids surrounding knotted proteins have not been explored in detail, the paper proposes fluid dynamics may influence their formation by shaping local chemical environments. To investigate this concept, the study converts the amino acid sequence of a knotted protein into an artificial three-dimensional random walk, incorporating a newly defined "fluid entropy" metric. By evaluating numerous three-dimensional random walk instances, researchers can identify a structure with the highest knotting probability, thereby selecting a unique three-dimensional random walk that retains inherent natural properties. This absolute topological framework does not rely on comparing artificial random walks to the complex native structure of a real knotted protein. Consequently, it provides an original method of node-based 3D random walk selection that exploits the proteins' intrinsic natural attributes.

We create three new symplectic mapping category groups, denoting the categories of symplectic maps for the blown-up complex symplectic planes within the four-dimensional torus, at specific locations, $ \Omega^2 T^2_\pm $, at distinct points, $ \Omega^2 T^2_0 $, and at two separated points, $\Omega^2 T^2_2 $, within the four-dimensional torus $T^2_\pm, T^2_0, T^2_2$. 
For any configuration of target domains, we demonstrate that the mapping between the symplectic categories of two such domains is independent of the particular choice of configuration, establishing the functorial nature of the symplectic mapping category. We also prove that the symplectic mapping category groups for these configurations are isomorphic to the integer groups at two points, $ \mathbb{Z}^2 $, and zero for domains with no points, in the context of dimension four. Furthermore, we establish the isomorphism of the symplectic mapping category groups, denoting the categories of symplectic maps for the blown-up complex symplectic planes, to the homology groups, denoting the homology of two two-dimensional spheres within the four-dimensional torus, at specific locations, at two points, in two dimensions, and zero at three dimensions.

A generalization of the Nambu-Goldstone theorem is introduced, addressing the production of irregular or type-B Nambu-Goldstone particles resulting from the spontaneous breaking of a global or gauge symmetry in both relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum field theories. A revised definition of the symmetry breaking pattern is required to properly classify the irregular type-B Nambu-Goldstone particles. A comprehensive, updated version of the "partial restoration" of symmetries is also necessary to explain the production of these particles. A complete account of the particle production process is derived from the effective Lagrangian theory, enabling the calculation of the partial symmetry restoration's temperature dependence.

Language models' poor counterfactual reasoning abilities are a significant issue that many researchers are working to resolve. Researchers have so far primarily focused on word-level counterfactuals, but the importance of phrasal-level counterfactuals in real-life scenarios has been overlooked. Our work defines and explores this underexamined aspect of counterfactual reasoning. An investigation into this matter reveals the limitations of an extensive language model's capacity to reason about complex, multi-step counterfactual situations. Our research also physically distinguishes between such scenarios with and without extensibility. To rectify this, our paper suggests a method for extracting phrasal counterfactuals from an extensive language model, utilizing its sentence simplification capabilities. Our work contributes to the fields of counterfactual reasoning and several related topics, including sentence paraphrasing, simple reasoning, and multi-step reasoning.

Epitaxial growth on graphene substrates has become valuable in directly producing functional materials due to its ability to enable various interfacial interactions, expanding its suitable applications. Through research, we discovered that by adjusting the size of the pinholes in the underlying graphene, we can control the suitable conditions for its use in van der Waals epitaxy. Our analysis of the interface showed that an ideal setup for this specific interfacial interaction can be achieved by pressing a (0001) sapphire onto an Al-rich (Cu,Al)₂MnSn sample. Furthermore, by changing the boiling point of alcohol, we developed a straightforward method to balance the distances of the aluminum layers and determined the optimal setup for pinhole van der Waals epitaxy.

This research is about a specific type of error-correcting code known as $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes, which are capable of detecting and correcting errors in transmitted data. The concept of a 'rank' has been introduced for these codes, which serves as a generalization of the rank for traditional $\mathbb{Z}_q$-linear codes. The properties of this rank have been explored in this study, along with the development of methods to create codes with specific, desired properties. The study also generalizes the concept of a dual code and a parity-check matrix, which are essential tools for analyzing these codes, and provides a definition for a class of codes that are characterized by their residue and digit components. The relationship between the concept of rank and the codimension of the codes' null space has been established as another key contribution of this study, which serves as a generalization of a previously established result.

Label Equitability is a new metric for evaluating supervised learning models, 
specifically evaluating a model's ability to generalize to underrepresented label 
categories. Our data hypothesis is that models' poor performance on labels with 
unseen instances hampers label equitability. To address this issue, our second 
goal is to create a method of evaluating the lexicographical order of labels in 
datasets and propose Label Order Awareness (LOA) as a metric and improvement 
strategy. Our results show that incorporating label order information through 
simple data augmentations can improve our proposed metric significantly and 
improve several established metrics on average.

We establish a 2-categorical isomorphism between the collection of functorctors that map from a monoid (G, *, 1) into the 2-category of 2-groups, into those that result from taking the opposite of G first, then a 2-categorical adjunction into the 2-group. This isomorphism leads to the identification of the resulting composite processes with a 2-categorical adjunction from the opposite of G into the 2-category of 2-groups.

The energy source behind galaxies with strong gamma-ray output remains unknown.
We propose that high-energy gamma-rays may originate from magnetic fields
trapping energetic cosmic rays within the vicinity of active galaxies.
In this scenario, the magnetic fields would have to possess extremely high
strengths, potentially captured during galaxy mergers with dwarf galaxies
having lofty central field strengths.
We discovered that our model effectively accounts for the gamma-ray data from
the nearby Andromeda galaxy and the Milky Way's neighbor M31, but makes a
testable prediction: we should observe similar gamma-ray and radio emissions
across the nearby local group of galaxies.

The goal of heart sound categorization is to accurately identify normal and abnormal heart sounds based on a heart sound signal. Any underlying disease can manifest as irregular acoustic patterns, making even mild abnormalities difficult to detect. In this study, we address normal and abnormal heart sound categorization, taking into account external sounds such as those caused by conversations or recording equipment vibrations, and significant signal distortion. We also investigate the impact of non-linear distortions, commonly found in field recordings, on heart sound categorization performance. To achieve this, we developed a robust feature extraction method using the YIN algorithm to accurately estimate fundamental frequency and its harmonic components, which served as inputs to a high-performance deep neural network classifier. To evaluate our approach, we used two well-known heart sound datasets, applying extensive signal distortion simulations to simulate real-world recording conditions, including both additive and convolutional distortions. Our results show that the proposed method is capable of effectively distinguishing normal and abnormal heart sounds, even under significant signal distortion.

The rapid expansion of cloud computing and wearable technology has made managing personal health data both feasible and common. Nevertheless, this process faces a major obstacle due to the lack of cloud trust. Wearable devices produce vast amounts of data, and sharing them among users can enhance accuracy and effectiveness in diagnosing and managing illnesses. Federated learning is well-suited for this task, enabling secure collaboration without compromising privacy. Unfortunately, FL's performance is limited when dealing with small datasets typical of wearable technology. To overcome this challenge, we propose FedHealth, a novel wearble personal healthcare framework that utilizes federated transfer knowledge. FedHealth leverages a shared structure to facilitate knowledge transfer among devices, facilitating collaborative modeling without compromising privacy. Our method has been experimentally validated using personal weight data from five wearable devices, accurately predicting four metabolic metabolic diseases with an $F_1$ score of 0.85.

This study examines three portfolio improvement methods based on "a a a" - a term used to denote various averages, specifically, the first and second moments, median, and mean. We establish a direct connection between two portfolio techniques, known as the tangential portfolio (TMPE) and the optimal portfolio (MPE), demonstrating that TMPE can be viewed as a higher-moment extension of MPE. Additionally, we provide a direct link between the portfolio technique based on the criterion of the second and the first conditional moments, developed by Elton, Bi, and Tsai (EBT), and the MPE framework, showing that the EBT approach is equivalent to MPE in certain circumstances, particularly when analyzing the option component of asset classes. The study also highlights the interplay among different portfolio theory frameworks.

This is an explanation of a system called a Agent, which that can perform various computer tasks, 
including using applications like web browsers and office software, with an focus on how it 
compares to existing methods, existing related work, and where it's heading in the future.

Consider a variation of the dual trading-betting problem where the agent's final wealth results from multiplying a return and the outcome of cashing in or purchasing an asset at zero cost, either through a button press or an arbitrary decision to keep or reset the device, accompanied by potentially discontinuous expenses after each action. Given that there is no cost for pressing the button, in order to maximize expected wealth, the problem calls for maximizing the expected product of returned funds and the number of successful trades, or, given that the number of trades is unlimited, the problem calls for maximizing the expected sum of logs of returned funds. With the asset modeled as a non-negative stochastic process and final wealth as a multiplicative product, both the trading-betting issue results in a toggling optimization that lacks general betafair solutions, and, under additional assumptions, can be solved into fair solutions that, though mathematically feasible, are not always optimal in maximizing expected wealth, ultimately calling for near-maximal betting-trading strategies.

The production of single leptoquarks via the b-quark initiated process at the LHC is being analyzed, taking into account the full leptoquark content. While the known leptoquarks that result from the electroweak symmetry breaking are well-documented, the production of other leptoquarks, which require supposing new physics, is also being considered, including those that could arise from string theory or GUT theories. It is important to note that the leptoquarks' properties, such as their masses and couplings, can significantly impact the expected rates of single leptoquark production, which, although generally low, are likely to be detectable at high-luminosity LHC experiments. Furthermore, even though the "known" leptoquarks may not be found at the current level of energy, they could play a crucial role in explaining certain particle physics anomalies, such as the non-leptonic B-meson decay anomalies, within effective field theory frameworks.

Observations often show that polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and carbon monoxide lines are under-saturated. We propose that non-thermal processes, specifically shock waves, may partially explain this observation. If this hypothesis is accurate, shock effects would primarily manifest in the lower energy lines of these molecules, which is consistent with typical stellar populations in galaxies. The sub-thermal excitation of these intensity lines can be modeled using non-LTE approaches. If our hypothesis is correct, the ratio between two specific transit wavelengths for single ionized carbon will provide an indicator of local gas temperature. This could be a valuable tool for researchers working with the ALMA telescope to better understand gas conditions in galaxies. However, if non-thermal processes are not dominant, this ratio will lack sensitivity to temperature changes.

We conducted simulations to generate pulsar timing array waveforms from merging pulsating binaries with high eccentricity, applying progressively stricter comparisons between numerical and analytical general relativity. Our process involved adjusting the phase of each numerical waveform to achieve the lowest possible phase residuals when using an analytical model, revealing that for a typical population of such binaries, the computational costs progressively rose as we tightened the tolerance for phase residuals. We discovered that with tighter Ties, there was a point of diminishing returns, where further improvements resulted in disproportionately high computational expenses. Our analysis showed that the majority of numerical genersators exceeded the computational expense of other, more efficient numerical genersators with only slightly more precise waveforms. This research provided precise, comprehensive waveforms from an eccentric binary merger and identified the optimal process for generating precise, low-error post-Newtonian waveforms for pulsar timing array analyses.

We establish a "velocity procedure" for ASEP that yields a unique way for ASEP particles to move based on the average speeds of neighboring particles in a sequential manner. This discovery enables us to characterize unique ways for the ASEP to move in one dimension with site boundaries, free boundaries, and two sources and two sinks; these ways are shown to preserve the Markov property, preserve the step and shock initial conditions, and they simulate the six vertex model's dynamics in the same manner. This allows us to examine how the asymptotic behavior of the typical shock's displacement either remains finite or grows polynomially or exponentially in time, depending on the velocities, and it also enables us to access existing asymptotic results as well as identify new ones in more symmetric cases where the distribution of the five asymptotic regions remains unknown in the long term.

Comprehensive epidemic modeling is crucial for effective management of outbreaks. Despite various criticisms, these models have been widely utilized in the ongoing SARS-CoV-2 outbreak. Compart mental models, which were once heavily dominated by frequency-dependent transmission, are being enhanced to incorporate other vital factors. These include growth-limiting behaviors exhibited by infected individuals, depletion of susceptible populations through super-spreading events, and spatial and temporal dynamics. Although integrating these dynamics presents significant complexities, their omission can lead to critical modeling inaccuracies.

Near Feshbach resonances, molecules formed from cold atoms can be induced to form through three-body recombination when a non-zero cross-section for loss occurs. Experimental observations showed significantly higher recombination coefficients for magnetic-stable molecules compared to atoms, with this difference varying greatly between experiments for the same species. To understand this complexity, a three-body scattering calculation based on a two-body calculation of loss cross-sections was conducted, with results indicating that the three-body scattering length is as large as $10^3$ times its typical value, explaining the exceptionally high recombination coefficients seen in molecule experiments.

A hierarchical information structure that organizes data into a tree shape is
basically the same as standard DNA storage, but with a key difference: in
hierarchical systems, index proteins are used to help locate and retrieve
hundreds of DNA pages within a storage system. While both systems rely on
chemistry to retrieve stored data, both the chemical processes in DNA storage
and the hierarchical structure require information that must be kept up to date
as they change over time. This paper focuses specifically on creating
hierarchy and updating the associated information in a practical and efficient
manner. It proposes a (hierarchical) page management system that handles
complex page operations by handling index proteins that form the hierarchy,
resulting in simpler biological processes. It also presents index protein
designs that can handle both hierarchy and information updates with
shortened DNA sequences, reducing synthesis costs. By incorporating
reversible binary coding, the proposed methods produce readable DNA sequences
that reduce errors during retrieval. Furthermore, this paper provides
theoretical foundations and practical guidelines for handling complex
hierarchical information in DNA storage by effectively managing index proteins.

Using PDE-driven deep learning, a novel approach is presented to solve the shallow water equations at pace, with a substantial test case involving an arbitrary lake basin and time-varying boundaries. Our method involves constructing a neural network to approximate the solution of the shallow water equations, ensuring high accuracy through a loss function that encompasses the residual of the differential equations and boundary conditions. While effective in simple scenarios, this basic model proved inadequate for a complex test case involving an irregular lake basin with irregular boundaries, prompting the development of a hybrid model with pre-trained components. This advanced model achieved remarkable accuracy, correctly predicting water depth and flow velocity with minimal error, and is anticipated to be of significant utility in hydrological modeling and oceanography.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at different exposure levels to expand the dynamic range and prevent overexposed or underexposed areas. Most existing research on exposure bracketing recommends taking three to nine images to ensure proper over- and underexposed areas. However, this approach may not always be necessary, as it depends on various factors such as scene characteristics, lighting conditions, and the algorithm used to fuse the images. This research proposes an algorithm that evaluates the current scene's dynamic range and automatically selects the optimal number of images to capture, thereby reducing the time required to take photos while ensuring high-quality results. Furthermore, the developed method was implemented on a smartphone to demonstrate its effectiveness in creating high-quality high-dynamic-range photos.

Neural networks are excelling in various tasks but struggle with certain capabilities that we expect from rational thought, such as generalizing from limited experiences and understanding cause-and-effect relationships to make predictions under new conditions. Although we anticipate causal neural learning to bridge this gap, current methods fail to consistently achieve this goal. In our study presented as a guide to causal neural learning, we aim to integrate diverse neural algorithms with theories of causal inference, addressing significant open challenges including prospective research directions. We start by defining the crucial differences between standard statistical learning and causal inference, then present examples of models that can be enhanced through causal frameworks and potential approaches to implement this integration. We also outline five settings that would facilitate actual deployment of such systems and propose five areas where the community should focus to advance causal neural learning.

This work introduces a new topological framework called the b-principle, which can be applied to a broader category of maps beyond those considered in traditional parametric intersection theory. We highlight two critical issues with our initial approach: one related to characteristic classes and the other, a partial solution involving a modified class called the beta-Mumford class, which satisfies key properties known as M1 through M4.

Understanding how fluids interact with deformable surfaces, known as fluid-structure interaction, requires solving complex equations that couple different variables. These equations are notorious for slowing down numerical simulations due to their difficult mathematical properties. To mitigate this challenge, researchers must carefully construct preconditioners that replicate the original problem's behavior in a scaled multilevel framework. This is essential for efficiently solving these problems using modern multilevel numerical methods. This work aims to further our understanding of cardiac mechanics by investigating and testing various preconditioning techniques across multiple scaled domains. Through numerical experiments, multiple architectural frameworks were compared to determine the most suitable framework for implementing this science. Furthermore, novel scalable architectures were proposed to better capture repulsive forces, and their performance was validated through rigorous multilevel simulations.

This study focuses on non-normal diffusion processes observed in materials with spatially varying properties. We developed two computational methods to analyze the movement of a random walker through such materials, utilizing simulations with spurious (artificial) and "realistic" representations of varying permeability fields. Through extensive simulations, we found that the root-mean-square displacement in these materials exhibits spatially-localized, sub-diffusive behavior. Our analysis reveals that the mean square displacement follows a $ \langle r^2(t)\rangle \sim t^\alpha $ pattern, with an exponent $\alpha \approx 1.3$ based on the initial conditions and a logarithmic correction derived from the distribution of local diffusion coefficients. The study also established the relationship between the distribution of these coefficients and an appropriate fractal dimension. Analytical estimates were validated through numerical evidence, even under more realistic, complex and multifractal spatial distributions of local diffusion coefficients often seen in geological and physical materials exhibiting spatial disorder.

A mathematical framework is developed to understand various optical reflection and transmission effects, including the Kerr nonlinear interaction between a resonator and a waveguide. The model incorporates key parameters such as coupling coefficients, waveguide group velocity, and refractive index modification caused by the Kerr effect. By deriving dispersionless models from derived expressions, we obtain formulas that predict the outcomes of non-ideal scenarios. Furthermore, explicit solutions to a defocusing non-linear Schrödinger equation are found, providing insights into optical solitons and their interaction with a lossy resonator.

Chaotic flow simulations offer a solid framework to study fluid dynamics, yet they often require post-processing to recover missing data due缺少 raw experimental data for direct comparison. Reconstructing high-resolution missing data from low-resolution images is a challenging task, especially given the inherent unpredictability of chaotic flow patterns. We employ generative adversarial networks to address this challenge and train them using a flow field from the Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection as an example, demonstrating significant success in recovering high-Reynolds number flow patterns. Our method effectively prevents mode contamination, a common issue in other reconstruction techniques, and successfully restores flow patterns corresponding to various Reynolds numbers.

DLTExplorer originally proposed as L2Explorer is a FRP based reinforcement learning assessment platform. Although RL libraries like Stable Baselines2 and Sacred have extensive PyTorch and TensorFlow evaluations for point-based games, PyGame-based continuous real-world tasks lack comparable structures. L2Explorer addresses this gap by providing comprehensive RL assessments for PyGame-based continuous real-world tasks like CartPole and MountainCar. The platform features modular design, incorporating aspects like assessment subjects, Sacred-based experiment management, Sacred logging, PyTorch modeling, Tmux/Sacred integrated terminal, and Forever learning concept. While present as a PyGame-based prototype, the DLC developers intend to extend the DLC ecosystem to encompass other assessment technologies like GANs and deep learning evaluations like GANs.

In this work, we introduce a new type of surveillance function for declarative
algorithms, with a specific focus on process models represented as collections of
conditions and actions. Our method incorporates external information derived from
non-recurring data sources, specifically for unusual cases that the existing
criteria fail to recognize, and also features an inherent exploration mechanism
to discover new rules from historical data, thereby improving the quality of
data integrated into revised models. Our approach involves using a progressive
mathematical framework for defining complex patterns beyond simple classifications,
and we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through various case studies.

The research focus is on extending a one-dimensional parameter space, specifically the unit sphere $S^1$, representing monic square polynomials with coefficients that are real numbers, in a comprehensive way. The goal is to identify the properties of the extended space, which includes all such polynomials. Initially, the space was defined by Jouanolou as the set of polynomials in two variables, but it was later recognized as the moment graph of J. H. Steele. The research reveals that this space is not compact and is equivalent to a specific type of star-shaped arrangement. The study provides all closed convex shapes that define this arrangement, which are in direct correlation with the combinatorial elements of the Apéry complex. The research also provides an explicit definition of the extended polynomials that make up the closure of the set of monic square polynomials, highlighting that this subset is significantly larger than the monic square polynomials whose roots are non-negative numbers.

The relationship between stars and star formation formation rate is influenced by SFR and stellar mass turnover points, which may signal transitions in physical processes. By examining local galaxies, we aim to identify the primary factor driving the behavior that changes at high masses, which may signal the role of star forming bulges. Utilizing K-band as a measure of star formation and disc and bulge components, we aim to test the hypothesis that star formation patterns change across different morphological types, consistent with observations indicating that quenching mechanisms also vary. Our analysis reveals that lower-energy stars continue to be formed in galaxies with b/d ratios of less than 1, which supports the notion that the turnover point results from the dominant energy of star formation in massive star forming bulges. We also found that star formation is more active in massive galaxies with a prominent bulge component, which may signal the need to consider supermassive black hole interactions on a case-by-case basis.

Capturing sentiment across different languages entails more than just conveying
approval or disapproval of an entity, it also conveys a specific language's
unique emotional tone.  This variation makes evaluating (multi)lingual
sentiment on unknown entities particularly challenging using traditional
methods.  Our analysis indicates that across-language sentiment evaluation
requires predicting both types of approval: the target domain's emotional
tone in the target language and emotional tone of the source language.  Thus,
a simple neural network can be trained on separate tasks using source and
target language data to evaluate the source language sentiment.  Our
approach's advantages include utilizing abundant source language data and
integrating both datasets to share linguistic and domain-specific features.  Our
approach is straightforward to apply for any source and target language
assessments where sufficient source language material is available, our
approach's efficacy is indicated by improved classification accuracy on four
cross-lingual sentiment assessment datasets.

Based on the hypothesis that data points can be categorized into groups with similar patterns, a few key features of ICU admissions in X-ray images of COVID-19 patients may be identifiable. Utilizing the K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) algorithm, a distinction is drawn between patients whose images show ICU admissions and those they do not. The research reveals that an 11% drop in contrast between X-ray images and an average increase in texture of 0.12 for left lungs, along with 0.15 for right lungs, are indicative of ICU admissions. These findings provide valuable insights for clinical settings, aiding in the identification of patients with severe COVID-19 and in need of ICU treatment.

The concept of a simplicial bundle was first introduced by D. E. Cohen in 1973, and it played a key role in solving the Conner-Scott problem. Since then, researchers have delved into the subject, but the underlying theorems remain abstract. The goal of this study is to convey the underlying theorems related to simplicial bundles in a more accessible manner, and to present the proof of the main theorems, and the Conner-Scott theorems, from first principles. Additionally, we will explain the relationship between simplicial bundles and local simplicial structures, and demonstrate that the global simplicial bundle is essentially a simplicial structure, up to certain equivalences.

This research focuses on establishing a visual association detection task, where successful completion requires models to accurately identify relationships between a given image and independent, unrelated images. Models that previously achieved success in related tasks, such as visual question answering, commonsense visual reasoning, and relationship prediction, were adapted and evaluated on this new task. Our baseline model, built upon a recent framework for visual reasoning with multiple objects, failed to complete the task effectively due to its tendency of incorrectly identifying associations with the given image. We examined the causes of this issue, categorized as "false positives," and proposed a new attention-suppression mechanism to mitigate its impact by reducing unnecessary relationships with irrelevant objects. When applied to our dataset, this mechanism successfully improved association detection rates between the target image and independent images.

Cosmological models suggest that major galaxy mergers fuel bulge galaxies at high rates, yet many bulge galaxies formed through calm processes. Our study of the $z\approx2.8$ galaxy cluster WHANAM-4 reveals calm mass asymmetries that fueled intense outer galaxy star formation and fueling of a central bulge which formed without a major galaxy merger. We track the movement of gas from the cluster's outskirts to the center, following the development of the host galaxy and the creation of a galaxy in the cluster. A large galaxy formation rate in the cluster's core led to internal bulge growth and the capture of a dwarf galaxy, followed by extensive baryonic fueling of the cluster's periphery, resulting in an uneven disk with internal and external star formation regions, and the re-accretion of gas fueling the central bulge. Buggy simulations match the arrangement of dark matter, gas, and stars in the cluster, and show that theoretical galaxy formation processes led to a small bulge-to-total mass ratio, an extensive disk mass, and a moderate mass asymmetry, in line with the measurements of Buggy data, giving support to bulge formation through quiet processes.

On November 7, 2004, a particularly energetic solar flare of X-class magnitude 4.3 was discovered in the sun's left side within the 111 stream. Following this, two bursts of solar neutrons were detected by NOAA's Space Environment Monitor-2 instrument. Using data from the GEOPRO-2 instrument, we analyzed the energy spectra of these solar particles in two energy ranges: high and low energy. The results showed that the low-energy spectrum consisted of two components, both associated with the main solar flare, while the high-energy spectrum was generated by a secondary solar flare that was later confirmed by other observations in the X-ray and radio frequency ranges.

The discovery of exoplanets by the ESO's Very Large Telescope, specifically the SPHERE facility, reveals remarkable angular momentum characteristics in the system of the star GJ 1252. Initially, the detection of a giant exoplanet through direct imaging, along with its wide orbital distance of about 2.6 astronomical units, was unexpected for a star with such high rotation speeds. Furthermore, the observed absorption features of the planet, including titanium oxide, water, and carbon monoxide, were also unusual for its temperature range, and did not match the predictions based on its atmospheric composition. This research explores two possible explanations for the abnormal angular momentum characteristics of the star, including the potential impact of the exoplanet on the star's characteristics through the tidal forces, and offers an alternative explanation involving an additional outer planet in the system with much larger orbital distance.

The rapid proliferation of news on the internet has given rise to a surge in counterfeit content, which poses a significant threat to public safety and social stability.  Automatic counterfeit news detection across multiple media types is a formidable challenge due the vast amount of unstructured and noisy data.  A supervised deep learning method would require extensive, annotated text-label pairs, which are rarely available in this domain.  To address this limitation, our research focuses on emerging multimodal counterfeit news detection using only unannotated clicking behavior.  We develop a novel emergent multimodal counterfeit news detector based on meta neural process networks, which lever_user_ clicking patterns from web pages, articles, and web banners to identify counterfeit news.  We structure and analyze a large multimodal dataset comprising web pages, news content, click patterns, and quality labels, which serves as the foundation for training and testing our emergent detector.  Our approach comprises two main phases: first, multi-task learning is employed to align the data modalities, and second, a meta detector is constructed to classify news as authentic or fake.  Our emergent multimodal counterfeit news detector outperforms state-of-the-art single-modal baselines in a fair single-modal comparison, and achieves superior performance in web-based counterfeit news detection according to rigorous evaluation criteria.

This research extends previous work on Golay complementary structures by developing a framework for polyphase designs. Whereas prior designs were limited to two phases, our approach accommod designs with four phases. We establish the conditions under which such four-phase Golay complementary structures can exist and proceed to create various designs, including those comprised of rectangular and circular elements. Notably, our search has yielded several unprecedented polynomials that lack a circular counterpart.

Crystalline silicon's low-disorder triple-minima potential gives rise to equivalent valleys with opposite effective charge orientations. When the symmetry is broken, the valleys begin to interact, and quantum tunneling between the valleys leads to the formation of two distinct energy sub-bands associated with the "plus" and "minus" effective charge states. This research investigates valley and spin current transmission through silicon-based quantum dot spin valves with coherent valley and spin channels, demonstrating that tunneling magnetoresistance can be observed for both types of currents and that both depend heavily on the geometry of the contacts and the crystallographic structure of the silicon. By systematically analyzing various factors, including magnetic adlayers, the orientation of the device within the silicon lattice, and isotopic silicon variants, we predict that both valley and spin currents in silicon molecular devices can exhibit TMR values in the hundreds of percent, potentially enabling extremely high-density and robust data storage technologies.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are widely used in various system analysis tasks, including classification, regression, and classification of nodes, edges, and entire graphs. However, GNNs often struggle to effectively model complex system dynamics underlying simple graph structures due to their tendency to prioritize local dependencies over global interactions. In many graph-based problems, the relationships between graph components and the overall system dynamics are inextricably linked, yet most current GNN frameworks attempt to learn these elements separately. This paper presents a unified Graph Neural Network architecture that simultaneously learns the structure and dynamics of complex systems, demonstrating its versatility through several applications, including a novel temporal interdependency graph framework, which achieves superior performance compared to the state-of-the-art in graph-based time series forecasting and variable selection tasks.

This paper introduces a specific type of partition, emerging from algebraic topology, derived from the structure of the set of edges in a 1-simplex within a certain topological space called a Barratt-Priddy-Quillen spectrum. By examining the connected components of this space's edges, we establish that each component is uniquely identified by a partition of the set of edges in the 1-simplex. Exploring topological properties, we determine that the 1-simplex's path components form a 1-dimensional graph structure, where the connectivity of this graph is related to specific mathematical concepts, resulting in the idea that an arbitrary partition can be generated through the action of a symmetric group, reflecting the relationship between algebraic K-theory and stable homotopy theory.

Brain lesions are abnormal formations in brain tissue that can take various shapes. They are often associated with diseases and injuries. In many cases, they are the result of illnesses like epilepsy and tumors. Sometimes, they are created artificially for research and development purposes in medical imaging. The generation of realistic cerebral lesions is an important task for training medical algorithms that detect and analyze these formations. A new technique has been devised to generate realistic cerebral lesions on healthy brain images. This approach uses an enhanced neural network, which uses a prior assumption that the created lesions are continuous and enclosed. The network is trained to meet multiple requirements, including staying within the image space, preserving the structure of the brain, and leaving certain areas of the brain untouched. The technique is able to generate images with lesions that are highly similar to real-world cerebral abnormalities, as shown by a comprehensive evaluation using multiple scoring methods. This approach is able to generate images with lesions that are easier to classify for a simple detector, as shown by the results of various experiments. The created network is also able to generate lesions on images with different resolutions and on images from different imaging devices. The overall quality of the created cerebral lesions is further demonstrated through various case images and their corresponding masks and structural components, as shown in the study's findings.

A significant improvement to the GP-2 Gaussian Process Regression compiler was made, reducing the computational workload when applying a precompiled model to new data. The original compiler generated Python code with computational tasks to locate necessary data within memory-addressed arrays. By creating a compiler that produces optimized C code, these memory location searches are eliminated. The resulting compiled binary lacks the GP-2 object, necessitating either recompilation with updated coefficients or manual entry of coefficients in Python for smaller datasets. The compiler also has the capability to incorporate basis functions beyond the existing two.

To facilitate extraction of additional information from existing embeddings, pretrained language models such as BERT were originally created. Although effective for specific tasks, this added flexibility also makes the models overly adaptable, resulting in poor generalization and added complexity for end-users. To address these limitations, we aim to develop a consistent framework for all possible extraction scenarios, focusing specifically on numerical attributes for natural language with BERT representations as the foundation. Our framework, which integrates contrastive learning to identify and link the original data with the embeddings, allows for easy addition of new attributes and employs a contrastive loss combined with a regression loss for training. Our approach, which is BERT's structure, demonstrates increased effectiveness compared to state-of-the-art methods that start with BERT's frozen representations, while also showcasing BERT's versatility within our unified framework.

Two new infinite families of quotient groups are identified that contain all star normal subgroups of the twisted wreath products $C_p \wr_T A_n}$, where $p$ is a prime number greater than or equal to 3 and the set $T$ has a size of $n-1$. Specifically, the first family, denoted as $\mathcal{F}_1$, comprises the twisted wreath product $W_p$ of the cyclic group of order $p$ within $C_p \wr_T T\}$, while the second family, denoted as $\mathcal{F}_2$, includes subgroups defined by the stabilizer of a point in the second coordinate and the cyclic group of order $p$ in its respective components.

For edge detection in graph-based data structures, sparsity-enhancing methods, such as the Graph Lasso, have been widely applied.  Nonetheless, a limitation arises with edge variables represented as categorical information, hindering direct application of these techniques.  This project aims to overcome this shortcoming, illustrated using a graph-based version of the Irish Poball Cuid (Ballroom) dataset.  By extending the Group Lasso method to categorical information via dummy variable expansion and maintaining dimensionality reduction, we developed the Graph Group Lasso method.  This new technique successfully identifies significant graph edges and demonstrated reliability in testing simulations.  It outperformed established alternatives, such as the Graph Lasso method, when applied to real-world data.

Large language models excelling in various tasks lack the ability to retain knowledge effectively between sessions. To address this limitation, the concept of Extreme Scale Retrieval was introduced, allowing these models to retain information externally in a efficient manner. This introduced method of ground-breaking scale retrieval, our newest breakthrough known as Skill Model, combines extensive LDMs with information that can be easily accessed. In contrast to traditional methods like prompt-based and weight injection, our innovative solution seamlessly integrates with various models and incorporates several new features like structured insights that enhance learning efficiency. Our extensive experiments using several EGSM training datasets and the Google BigCode StarCoder model showcase the exceptional effectiveness of this new model, achieving precise results with the help of a small number of neural network components.

When lines are drawn between points on vector maps, the lines may partially extend beyond their intended width due to anti-aliasing effects, resulting in a perceived loss of accuracy. This issue, though rarely problematic, can significantly affect the reliability of representations that require precise spatial accuracy, such as land plots or property lines in real estate listings. The root cause of this effect is that anti-aliasing results in the drawn lines representing slightly narrower features than they should, effectively shifting the lines outward by approximately half a pixel's width. To rectify this effect, we propose an efficient and computationally inexpensive pre-rendering technique that eliminates anti-aliasing effects without compromising the benefits of vector maps. Our proposed technique achieves this effect removal, offering a near-zero performance overhead compared to the standard rendering procedure.

The drawback of this approach is the limited wearability and comfort due to the number of microphones required.
A single-microphone head-mounted device is more comfortable to use, yet it suffers from poor sound quality as a result of both desired speech and interference from other active sources.
The challenge of real-time processing for deep learning models hinders the use of such approaches in this scenario, as a result.
The necessity of using heavy models with numerous parameters further exacerbates the challenge of real-time inference for these approaches as a result.
In contrast, our Dual-Path Convolutional Recurrent Network (DPCRN) ensures both real-time inference for multiple simultaneous calls while delivering superior performance to the state-of-the-art methods, as a result.
The DPCRN divides the input speech signals into narrow and wide bands that are fed into distinct network branches with different numbers of parameters, as a result.
The output of both branches is combined in the time domain to produce the final result, yet, as a result.
The benefits of our approach are twofold: it gives us the flexibility to utilize separate network structures for different frequency bands as a result.
The light-weight small narrow-band network enables real-time inference for multiple simultaneous calls, as a result.
